➡️From Vintage to MNTGE: Digital Fashion Brand to Release NFT Patches Linked to IRL Rewards

Digital fashion brand MNTGE is gearing up to release its Patchwork collection, comprised of a series of non-fungible token (NFT) patches paired with a physical counterpart.

MNTGE Patchwork features 13 unique digital patches designed by 11 artists including Jen Stark, Bored Ape Yacht Club artist Seneca and Nyan Cat meme creator Christopher Torres. The entire 7,500-unit collection will open for sale on July 27 on NFT marketplace OpenSea. Each NFT will be priced at 0.07 ETH, or $130, and the artwork will be revealed upon mint.

Each NFT is linked to an identical physical patch. Embedded with a near-field communication (NFC) chip, owners can scan the real-world patch to claim the digital token in their crypto wallet. By holding the patch on the blockchain and IRL, users can trace ownership as well as attend token-gated events and exclusive MNTGE experiences.

Additionally, the patches aren’t just one-off collectibles. In the physical world, they can be sewn onto MNTGE’s “base garments,” including t-shirts, jackets and denim. In the digital realm, the patches can be “owned” by the base garment itself. By implementing an ERC-6551 token standard, the digital wearable becomes a token-bound account that can custody the patches – creating an added layer of digital ownership.

Nick Adler, co-founder of MNTGE, told CoinDesk that the company was rooted in the goal of selling vintage fashion and utilizing the blockchain to revitalize its origins.

“People are out there wearing [vintage] and collecting it…young kids want to be authentic,” said Adler. “They don't want a Hot Topic shirt, they want the original shirt, right? So we just saw this natural, really honest use case for the blockchain, and we just felt like the two could really go hand in hand.”

🔴 You're not living in 3 dimensions.

You've never lived.

A high school student just proved why everything you've learned about reality is incomplete.

Ready for this mind-bender:

Look at any object around you. A cup, a book, or even your phone will do. Now notice that it's casting a shadow, and that shadow is always flatter than the object itself. A 3D cup on your table makes a 2D shadow. A 2D piece of paper held up to the light creates a 1D line on the wall. Every dimension casts a flatter version of itself down into the lower dimension.

Now reverse that idea.

If your body is 3D and the pattern always works the same way, your body could be the shadow of a 4D thing you can't see.

In other words, you might not be the real thing.

There's a shape that describes this, called a tesseract. A cube is six flat squares folded together. A tesseract is eight cubes folded together in a direction that doesn't exist in our world. You can't imagine it. No one can. Your brain evolved to help your ancestors escape tigers and find fruit, not to picture shapes in dimensions we can't walk through.

When you try to imagine a tesseract, you're actually just seeing its 3D shadow; just like an ant crawling on a piece of paper can only see the straight lines of your hand, never the real hand itself.

If every solid thing is actually the lower-dimensional shadow of something bigger, a bunch of weird science suddenly starts to make sense.

Tiny particles appearing in two places at once aren't magic. They're just a single 4D object leaving two shadows in our 3D world.

Particles on opposite sides of the universe reacting to each other instantly aren't spooky at all, if they're actually one object touching our reality at two different points; like how a finger dipped in water looks like two separate spots to a bug living on the surface.

There's an old thought experiment that helps you get this.

Imagine a creature living on a completely flat piece of paper. It only knows left, right, forward, and back. It has no clue that "up" exists. Now push your finger down through the paper. To that creature, a circle appears out of nowhere, grows, shrinks, then vanishes. It spends its whole life trying to explain what it is. It invents theories, argues with other flat creatures, maybe even calls it a miracle. It would never guess it's a finger, because "up" is a direction its brain literally can't comprehend.

We're that flat creature. The weird stuff scientists see in experiments could be fingers poking into our world from a direction we can't look.

What that high school student explained so well is the limit of what your eyes and brain are allowed to see of reality.

📌 Tehran, IRNA — In a meeting with the ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Prime Minister of Cambodia condemned the recent US-Israeli aggression against Iran and the violation of international principles and values; and described the arrival of the new Iranian ambassador in Phnom Penh as the start of a significant new phase in cooperation between the two nations while stressing the expansion of bilateral relations.

Akbar Ghasemi, the Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to Cambodia, met with the country's Prime Minister, Hun Manet, and discussed ways to expand relations in the political, economic, agricultural, technological, cultural, and tourism sectors, as well as convening the two countries' joint economic commission.
​
Welcoming the Iranian ambassador to Phnom Penh, the Prime Minister of Cambodia described his presence as the start of a significant new phase in bilateral cooperation and expressed hope that substantial strides would be made during this period to enhance cooperation between the two countries.
​
Hun Manet also condemned the recent aggression against the Islamic Republic of Iran, describing the country as an aggrieved nation that has come under attack.
​
He characterized the act as a blatant violation of international principles and values ​​and, while condemning the martyrdom of the Islamic Republic of Iran's leader, expressed his solidarity with the Iranian people.
​
Welcoming the activation of exchanges between the public and private sectors of the two countries, the Prime Minister of Cambodia expressed interest in convening a joint economic commission and called for the activation of political and economic committees through the two countries' foreign ministries to achieve this goal.
​
The Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran, for his part, while conveying the greetings of Mohammad Reza Aref—Iran’s First Vice President—to the Prime Minister of Cambodia, expressed hope that—in light of new developments in West Asia and East Asia regions and given the significant potential for synergy between the Islamic Republic of Iran and Cambodia’s development projects—Iranian technical and engineering service companies, business owners, and commercial actors would play an active role.
​
Ghasemi also called for the convening of the political committee, the economic commission, and meetings between businesspeople and investors, as well as the holding of joint exhibitions between the two countries, within the framework of the new phase of relations between the Islamic Republic of Iran and Cambodia.
